occlude

uh-KLOOD · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To occlude is to stop up or completely close off (a passage, opening, or view).

The technician warned that dust and grime had begun to occlude the camera lens, leaving every photo hazy.

Worked Example

A dense stand of pine trees had grown up along the ridge, occluding the view of the valley that the cabin's owners once enjoyed from their porch.

The trees didn't destroy the valley -- they simply grew tall enough to block the line of sight to it, which is exactly what occlude means: to close off or obstruct.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

block: To block is the everyday, general word for stopping something from passing through, and a blockage can be partial -- a fallen branch can block a path while walkers still squeeze past. To occlude is more complete and more technical: it means to close a passage, opening, or view off entirely.

clog: To clog is to block a passage gradually, by filling it with built-up matter -- hair clogs a drain, grease clogs a pipe. To occlude says nothing about buildup; it simply means the passage, opening, or view ends up completely closed off, whatever did the closing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unblock: to clear a passage so it can flow again

expose: to leave open or uncovered

Where it sits · how completely the passage is blocked — narrow → occlude → seal

narrow vs. occlude: To narrow a passage is only to make it smaller -- a milder change than to occlude it, which closes the passage off completely so that nothing gets through at all.

seal vs. occlude: To seal something is to close it completely and permanently, an even more total blockage than occlude usually implies.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — oc- (ob-)

prefix — oc- (ob-): against, in the way of (Latin)

root — -clude (claudere)

root — -clude (claudere): to shut, to close (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Occlude comes from Latin ob- ('against, in the way') + claudere ('to shut') -- literally 'to shut against,' which came to mean blocking or closing off a passage.

Use the root in a new word: exclude

Use the root in a new word: exclude: The strict dress code was meant to exclude anyone not wearing the required uniform.

Root Check

Word Choice

Occlude is most often used in physical, medical, or scientific contexts -- a blocked artery, a blocked lens, a blocked view -- rather than for stopping a plan or idea, which is usually thwarted or stymied instead.
